abstract: |
  This study asks whether a researcher-level fixed effect estimated from bibliometric panel data reflects individual ability or a persistent, environment-driven component of the researcher's surroundings. Using the publication histories of 9,843 researchers in the top six economics journals (1970--2016), I estimate a time-invariant human-capital proxy from a cohort-percentile citation panel and design a test that separates a researcher's actual coauthors, whose quality is endogenous to the researcher's own ability, from researchers who were merely co-located at the same institution in the same years but never coauthored. A researcher-level fixed effect estimated from panel data on citations, output, or pay is routinely interpreted as a portable, time-invariant measure of individual ability. But such an effect is estimated jointly with a time-varying environment---coauthors, institutions, funding, and networks---that the individual does not fully choose and that may itself shape realized performance. Whether the estimated effect reflects ability net of this environment, or is contaminated by a persistent environmental component, is rarely tested directly, because a researcher's environment is typically chosen in a way that is correlated with their own unobserved ability, confounding any simple comparison.

This study develops a test that separates these two possibilities using the publication histories of the top six economics journals---*American Economic Review*, *Econometrica*, *Journal of Political Economy*, *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, *Review of Economic Studies*, and *Review of Economics and Statistics* (hereafter T6). After estimating a time-invariant human-capital proxy for each of 9,843 researchers (1970--2016), I compare researchers' actual early-career coauthors, whose quality is endogenous to the researcher's own ability, to researchers who were merely co-located at the same institution in the same years but never coauthored---a source of exposure to peer quality that is far less correlated with a researcher's own ability. A researcher's own long-run performance is then regressed on this peer-quality measure with and without an institution fixed effect, isolating a within-institution effect of peer quality from a between-institution confound common to all researchers at historically strong institutions.

The same T6 panel also supports a brief secondary check of whether the early-1990s diffusion of information and communication technology (ICT) reshaped who succeeds in top-journal publishing, distinguishing a *returns channel* (ICT raises the ability premium) from a *threshold channel* (ICT lowers the cost of T6 entry). This check is included because it motivated the panel's original construction, but it is secondary to the paper's main question and its results are more tentative.

This study's central contribution adapts the logic of [@azoulay_zivin_wang2010]'s exogenous-shock peer-effects design to a co-location rather than a coauthorship comparison, providing direct evidence that early-career exposure to strong peers operates through resource congestion rather than a positive ability spillover, once institutional prestige is netted out. It also applies the interactive fixed-effects factor model of [@Bai2009] to economics T6 publication histories to construct the human-capital proxy this test relies on, and formally shows that a simpler additive alternative performs equally well out of sample. The secondary ICT check reinterprets the 1990s transition in economics research documented by [@Hamermesh2013] and [@angrist_etal2020] from the perspective of micro-level researcher cohorts entering T6 before versus after 1992.

# Literature Review {#sec-literature}

This study relates to three strands of the literature. The first pertains to the peer-effects and exogenous-shock literature on how a researcher's environment shapes measured performance. The second concerns methodological research on measuring researcher-specific time-invariant ability from panel citation data. The third examines citation patterns in economics and the 1990s turning point, relevant to this paper's secondary ICT check.

[@azoulay_zivin_wang2010] use the sudden deaths of eminent scientists as an exogenous shock to their collaborators' research environment and find that surviving coauthors' subsequent output declines, a pattern the authors attribute to the loss of access to the deceased superstar's resources and networks rather than to a loss of inspiration alone. This literature motivates the central methodological concern of this study: any procedure that infers ability from an individual fixed effect estimated jointly with a time-varying collaboration environment risks capturing the quality of researchers around an individual rather than a purely time-invariant personal trait. Section V develops a design that exploits co-location without actual coauthorship to isolate this concern from genuine assortative matching on ability, extending [@azoulay_zivin_wang2010]'s exit-based shock to an entry-based comparison.

[@Bai2009] proposes a panel data model in which the outcome of unit $i$ at time $t$ is decomposed into a unit-specific loading $\lambda_i$ interacted with a common time factor $F_t$, in addition to conventional additive fixed effects. Unlike an additive two-way fixed-effects model, the interactive specification $Y_{it}=\lambda_i F_t+\varepsilon_{it}$ allows the shape of the common time profile, not merely its level, to be scaled differently across units, and is estimated by iterative principal components on the (possibly incomplete) outcome matrix. This provides the theoretical basis for the human-capital proxy---the loading $\hat\lambda_i$, or, where the added flexibility is not empirically warranted, the additive author fixed effect $\hat\alpha_i$---whose origins the peer-environment design interrogates. Section III develops both specifications and selects between them on out-of-sample predictive grounds. [@angrist_diederichs2024] estimate the production function of citation outcomes at the economics doctoral dissertation level and show that observable inputs explain only a fraction of the performance variance; the present study absorbs part of this residual variation through $\hat\alpha_i$ and directly tests, in Section VI.C, how much of it reflects a persistent institutional environment rather than the individual alone.

[@Hamermesh2013] analyzes 60 years of publication patterns in the top three economics journals and shows that the point at which empirical research overtook theoretical research was the early 1990s, coinciding with the mass diffusion of ICT; this motivates the 1992 cohort demarcation used in Section VI.D's secondary check. [@hamermesh2018] discusses the usefulness of a 10-year citation window in reducing truncation bias for junior researchers, motivating this study's citation measure. [@angrist_etal2020] show that citations from outside the discipline to economics papers increased substantially after the 1990s, suggesting post-ICT citation changes reflect the broadening of interdisciplinary influence and not only within-field scale expansion.

# Theoretical Framework {#sec-theory}

## Ability, Technology, and Resources

A researcher's citation outcome is taken to depend on three conceptually distinct inputs: time-invariant human capital $H_i$ (the researcher's own ability), the period-specific technological environment $T_t$ (data access, computation, and dissemination infrastructure common to all researchers at a point in time), and time-varying research resources $K_{i,t}$, including institutional prestige and coauthor networks. This distinction serves two purposes below. First, because raw citation counts are also driven by secular growth in the size of the citing literature---an artifact of $T_t$ rather than of $H_i$---this study normalizes citation counts before estimation: each paper's 10-year citation count is converted into its percentile rank among all papers published in the same calendar year (Section III.A), so that the estimated author-level parameter reflects standing relative to same-vintage peers rather than the vintage itself. Second, the distinction between $H_i$ and $K_{i,t}$ is used directly in Section VI.C to ask whether the estimated author effect reflects ability alone or a persistent, resource-driven component of a researcher's environment.

## A Secondary Question: Two Channels for a Technology Shock

Within this framework, a technology shock like ICT diffusion could affect citation outcomes through two channels. The *returns channel* posits that ICT complements high-ability researchers, amplifying the ability premium (consistent with skill-biased technological change); it predicts a discrete, economy-wide citation-level shock timed to diffusion. The *threshold channel* posits instead that ICT lowers the cost of the data, software, and communication infrastructure needed to reach T6, expanding the *entering* cohort's ability distribution without necessarily changing the return to ability. Section VI.D tests both directly using the T6 panel and finds a wider entering-cohort distribution but no discrete level shock and no increased return to team size---more consistent with a compositional shift in entry than a clean instance of either channel, though the tests used are narrow (Section VI.D elaborates).

# Statistical Methods {#sec-methods}

## Cohort-Percentile Normalization {#sec-pctile}

For each paper $p$ published in calendar year $y(p)$, let $c_p$ denote its 10-year cumulative citation count. The cohort percentile is

$$
\text{pctile}_p \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{rank}(c_p \mid y(p))}{N_{y(p)}},
$$ {#eq-pctile}

where the rank is taken among all sample papers published in the same calendar year $y(p)$ and $N_{y(p)}$ is the size of that publication-year cohort. Author--academic-age cells are then formed by averaging $\text{pctile}_p$ over all papers a given author published at a given academic age $a_{i,t}=t-\text{first}_i$. This construction places every calendar era on the same 0--1 scale of relative standing and, by design, cannot detect a shock that shifts an entire publication-year cohort's citation level uniformly; Section VI.D therefore supplements it with a level-based specification for that narrow purpose.

## The Interactive Fixed-Effects Model {#sec-ife}

Let $Y_{it}$ denote the cohort-percentile outcome of author $i$ at academic age $t\in\{0,\dots,30\}$. Following [@Bai2009], the baseline specification is

$$
Y_{it} \;=\; \lambda_i F_t + \varepsilon_{it},
$$ {#eq-ife}

where $\lambda_i$ is a researcher-specific loading interpreted as time-invariant human capital and $F_t$ is a common academic-age profile shared by all researchers. Because the author--age panel is sparse (only academic ages at which an author actually published are observed), (@eq-ife) is estimated by a hard-impute algorithm: missing cells are initialized at the sample mean, a rank-one singular value decomposition of the resulting complete matrix is computed, missing cells are replaced by the low-rank reconstruction while observed cells are reset to their true values, and the procedure iterates to convergence. By the Eckart--Young theorem, each iteration solves the least-squares rank-one approximation problem exactly conditional on the current fill-in, so the procedure is a matrix-completion analogue of [@Bai2009]'s iterative principal-components estimator. Because the product $\lambda_i F_t$ is invariant to rescaling $(\lambda_i,F_t)\mapsto(c\lambda_i,F_t/c)$, the sign of $F_t$ is fixed so that its mean is positive, and $\hat\lambda_i$ is reported as a percentile rank across authors rather than in its native (arbitrary) scale.

## Model Selection: An Additive Alternative {#sec-modelselect}

The interactive specification (@eq-ife) is strictly more flexible than, and nests as a special case, the additive two-way fixed-effects model

$$
Y_{it} \;=\; \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_{it},
$$ {#eq-additive}

in which every researcher is assumed to share an identical academic-age profile $\gamma_t$ up to a level shift $\alpha_i$, rather than a profile that can also be rescaled in shape by $\lambda_i$. Because the additional flexibility of (@eq-ife) carries an identification cost---the sign and rotation indeterminacy of factor models, and a higher effective parameter count per author when extended beyond rank one---this study selects between the two specifications on the basis of five-fold out-of-sample cross-validation over observed author--age cells, rather than by in-sample fit alone. Held-out cells are masked as unobserved during re-estimation, and predictive $R^2$ is computed against a held-out-mean benchmark. This comparison, together with a null-data placebo check, is reported in Section VI.B; the additive specification (@eq-additive) is preferred throughout the remainder of the paper on the strength of that comparison, and $\hat\alpha_i$ is used as the primary human-capital proxy.

# Data {#sec-data}

## Data Sources

The publication data for this study were collected in three stages through the Elsevier Scopus API. First, metadata for article and review categories from the six T6 journals published since 1970 were collected, identifying 13,287 unique authors. Second, the complete publication histories of these authors, including non-T6 publications, were tracked to construct a panel of 431,874 author--paper rows corresponding to 335,558 unique papers. Third, the Scopus CitationOverview API was used to compute 10-year cumulative citations for each paper after publication.

## Construction of the Analytic Sample

Author--academic-age cells were formed for academic ages 0 through 30 using the cohort-percentile outcome of Section III.A, averaging multiple papers published by the same author at the same academic age into a single cell. Authors observed at fewer than two distinct academic ages---for whom author and academic-age effects cannot be jointly identified---were dropped. This restriction reduces the 13,287 T6 authors to a final analytic sample of 9,843 authors, observed in 112,091 of $9{,}843\times31=305{,}133$ possible author--age cells (36.7% density).

## Unit of Analysis and Dependent Variable

The unit of analysis is the combination of author $i$ and academic age $t$ (Sections III.A--III.B), except in the calendar-year specification of Section VI.D, which indexes observations by calendar year and uses $\ln(1+c_{i,t})$ rather than the cohort percentile, since the percentile transform is by construction invariant to a shock that shifts an entire cohort uniformly.

# Empirical Strategy: Separating Ability from Resource Congestion {#sec-strategy}

To test whether $\hat\alpha_i$ reflects time-invariant ability $H_i$ or a persistent, resource-driven component of $K_{i,t}$, two peer-quality measures are constructed from each author's first four academic-age years ($a_{i,t}\in\{0,1,2,3\}$). The first, $\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{coauth}}$, is the mean $\hat\alpha$ of an author's actual early-career coauthors. Because coauthor choice is endogenous to ability, a second, more plausibly exogenous measure, $\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{peer}}$, is constructed from researchers who published from the *same institution in the same or an adjacent calendar year* as the focal author but who never coauthored with that author at any point in either researcher's career. Both measures are regressed on the author's own long-run (academic ages 15--25) cohort-percentile performance, controlling for the author's own early-career (academic ages 0--3) performance, with and without a fixed effect for the author's modal early-career institution. Following the logic of [@azoulay_zivin_wang2010], comparing the pooled and within-institution estimates isolates a genuine peer-to-peer effect from a confound common to all researchers at historically strong institutions.

# Estimation Results {#sec-results}

## Basic Properties of the $\hat\alpha_i$ Distribution

Estimating (@eq-additive) on the full analytic sample recovers $\hat\alpha_i$ for all 9,843 authors. The distribution has a mean of $-0.006$, a median of $-0.007$, and a standard deviation of $0.154$, with mild positive skewness (0.21) and near-zero excess kurtosis ($-0.02$); a Shapiro--Wilk test on a random subsample of 5,000 authors gives $W=0.994$. Summary statistics are reported in @tbl-alpha-dist.

| Mean                    | $-0.006$ |
| Median                  | $-0.007$ |
| Standard deviation      |    0.154 |
| Minimum                 | $-0.367$ |
| Maximum                 | $+0.583$ |
| Skewness                |   $+0.21$ |
| Excess kurtosis         |   $-0.02$ |
| Shapiro--Wilk statistic ($n=5{,}000$) | $0.994$ |

## Model Selection: Interactive versus Additive Specifications {#sec-results-modelselect}

@tbl-modelselect compares the in-sample and five-fold out-of-sample $R^2$ of the interactive model (@eq-ife) and the additive model (@eq-additive), together with two uninformative benchmarks (an author-mean-only and an academic-age-mean-only predictor) and a placebo check in which the observed cohort-percentile values are randomly permuted across author--age cells before re-estimation, holding the missingness pattern fixed.

| Model | In-sample $R^2$ | Out-of-sample $R^2$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| Author-mean only | -- | 0.102 |
| Academic-age-mean only | -- | 0.031 |
| Additive, $\alpha_i+\gamma_t$ | 0.308 | **0.132** |
| Interactive, $\lambda_iF_t$ ($r=1$) | 0.308 | 0.132 |
| Placebo (randomly permuted values) | 0.087 | $-0.132$ |

: Model comparison via five-fold out-of-sample cross-validation {#tbl-modelselect}

Three results are notable. First, the interactive and additive specifications are statistically indistinguishable both in-sample (0.308 versus 0.308) and out-of-sample (0.132 versus 0.132), so the added rotation and scale indeterminacy of the interactive model buys no measurable predictive power in this application; the additive $\hat\alpha_i$ is used as the primary human-capital proxy for the remainder of the paper. Second, both specifications substantially outperform either uninformative benchmark, confirming that both author identity and academic age carry genuine, complementary information. Third, the placebo comparison shows that a positive in-sample $R^2$ (0.087) can arise from pure overfitting of the many per-author free parameters even when the underlying data contain no signal, but that this apparent fit collapses to a negative out-of-sample $R^2$ ($-0.132$); because the real-data out-of-sample $R^2$ remains reliably positive (0.132), the fitted model is judged to capture genuine, generalizable structure rather than an artifact of its flexibility. Since the author-level flexibility that lets the placebo overfit is equally present in the real-data specification, the in-sample figure of 0.308 should be read as an overstatement of genuine predictive content; 0.132 is the defensible estimate of the model's explanatory power.

## Peer Environment and the Origins of $\hat\alpha_i$ {#sec-results-peer}

@tbl-peer-effects reports the peer-environment design of Section V in three progressively more demanding specifications of

$$
\text{pctile}_i^{\text{late}} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{pctile}_i^{\text{early}} + \beta_2\,\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{peer or coauth}} + \eta_{j(i)} + u_i,
$$ {#eq-peer-spec}

where $\eta_{j(i)}$ is a fixed effect for the author's modal early-career institution.

| Spec. | Peer measure | Own early coef. | Peer coef. | $N$ | Institutions | $R^2$ |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| (1) Coauthors | $\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{coauth}}$ | 0.062\* | 0.245\*\*\* | 2,733 | -- | 0.032 |
| (2) Co-located | $\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{peer}}$ | 0.121\*\*\* | 0.173\*\*\* | 3,923 | -- | 0.021 |
| (3) Institution FE | $\overline{\alpha}_i^{\text{peer}}$ | 0.116\*\*\* | $-0.358$\*\*\* | 3,923 | 420 | 0.024 (within) |

: Progressive robustness of the early-career peer-quality coefficient in (@eq-peer-spec) {#tbl-peer-effects}

```{=latex}
\tablenote{\textit{Note}: *$p<0.05$, **$p<0.01$, ***$p<0.001$. Specification (1) restricts the peer measure to an author's actual coauthors on papers published at academic age 0--3 and controls for own early-career percentile alone (unconditional own-effect coefficient, not tabulated, is 0.104). Specifications (2)--(3) replace this with the mean ability of co-located but never-coauthored researchers observed at the same institution-year cells. Specification (3) additionally absorbs institution fixed effects, so identification rests solely on within-institution variation in peer quality across cohorts entering the same institution at different times.}
```

Two patterns emerge. First, moving from actual coauthors to co-located non-coauthors leaves the coefficient on own early-career performance essentially unchanged (0.121 versus 0.116 across specifications (2)--(3)), whereas including actual coauthor quality roughly halves it (from an unconditional 0.104 to 0.062 in specification (1)); this is consistent with actual-coauthor quality partly proxying for the focal author's own unobserved early-career ability, whereas co-located peer quality---which correlates with own early performance at only $r=0.060$, against $r=0.316$ for actual coauthors---constitutes a comparatively independent and more plausibly exogenous source of variation.

Second, and more strikingly, the sign of the peer-quality coefficient reverses once institution fixed effects are introduced, from $+0.173$ ($p<0.001$) to $-0.358$ ($p<0.001$). The pooled, between-institution estimate is consistent with a simple confound: institutions with historically strong faculty or resources produce both stronger co-located peer pools and stronger long-run outcomes for reasons unrelated to any peer-to-peer transfer of ability. Once this between-institution channel is removed, the within-institution estimate indicates that researchers who happen to enter a given institution during a cohort with an unusually strong contemporaneous peer pool exhibit *worse* long-run relative performance, holding their own early-career percentile fixed. This pattern is consistent with a congestion, or "big fish in a small pond," mechanism, in which a stronger local cohort intensifies competition for scarce mentorship, coauthorship, and visibility resources within $K_{i,t}$, rather than generating a positive knowledge spillover into $H_i$---directly paralleling the resource-loss interpretation of [@azoulay_zivin_wang2010], but operating through crowding at entry rather than through the exit of a senior collaborator. The reversal itself is the paper's central methodological point: the naive, between-institution comparison alone would have supported the *opposite* conclusion (a positive spillover), underscoring how easily unobserved institutional confounds can flip the sign of an apparent peer effect.

This result qualifies the structural interpretation of $\hat\alpha_i$ used throughout the paper: part of its cross-sectional variation reflects a persistent, environment-driven component of $K_{i,t}$, operating in a congestion rather than a complementary direction, rather than solely time-invariant ability $H_i$.

## Secondary Application: Cohort, Heterogeneity, and Calendar-Time Results {#sec-results-ict}

This subsection reports two narrow ICT tests, described here rather than in Section V because they are secondary to the paper's question: as noted in Section II.B, they speak only to a discrete level shock and to the team-size channel specifically, not to a general change in the return to ability.

The first splits authors by whether their *first T6-journal* publication---distinct from their first publication in any journal, which defines academic age---came before 1992 or in/after it, following [@Hamermesh2013]'s early-1990s breakpoint: 1,919 incumbents ($C^1$) versus 7,924 new entrants ($C^2$). Estimating (@eq-additive) separately within each cohort, @tbl-cohort-summary compares the resulting $\hat\alpha_i$ distributions. A two-sample Kolmogorov--Smirnov test rejects equality ($D=0.067$, $p=1.6\times10^{-6}$), and the standard deviation is 18.3% larger post-1992 (0.135 versus 0.160); the same pattern holds for the interactive loading $\hat\lambda_i$ (SD 0.713 versus 0.911, $D=0.075$, $p=6.2\times10^{-8}$), so it is not an artifact of the model-selection choice in Section III.C. Because $C^1$/$C^2$ are defined by entry cohort rather than a fixed calendar date, this comparison alone cannot separate a genuine period effect from an ordinary age-cohort pattern in which more recent entrants are earlier in their careers and hence more heterogeneous.

| Statistic | $C^1$ incumbent (pre-1992) | $C^2$ new T6 (post-1992) |
|---|---:|---:|
| $N$ | 1,919 | 7,924 |
| Mean $\hat\alpha_i$ | $-0.019$ | $-0.001$ |
| SD $\hat\alpha_i$ | 0.135 | **0.160** |

: $\hat\alpha_i$ distribution by T6-entry cohort {#tbl-cohort-summary}

@tbl-subgroup stratifies this comparison by collaboration structure. The widening is roughly uniform across international-collaboration subgroups (16.7% versus 20.4%) but markedly larger among large-team collaborators (21.5% versus 14.3%). However, a direct interaction regression of $\hat\alpha_i$ on mean team size, a post-1993 T6-entry indicator, and their interaction finds no significant change in the *return* to team size (interaction coefficient $-0.004$, $p=0.23$): teams grew larger, but collaborating in a larger team did not become significantly more rewarded. The subgroup pattern is therefore better read as corroborating a cohort-level compositional shift than as evidence on the return to ability itself.

| Subgroup | Pre-1992 SD | Post-1992 SD | \% increase |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| High international collaboration | 0.136 | 0.158 | 16.7% |
| Low international collaboration | 0.135 | 0.163 | 20.4% |
| Small collaboration team | 0.135 | 0.154 | 14.3% |
| **Large collaboration team** | 0.133 | **0.162** | **21.5%** |

: Growth in $\hat\alpha_i$ dispersion by collaboration subgroup {#tbl-subgroup}

The second test addresses the fact that the cohort-percentile outcome cannot, by construction, detect a shock common to an entire publication-year cohort. A level-based specification with an explicit calendar-year fixed effect is therefore estimated jointly with the rank-one interactive age factor,

$$
\ln(1+c_{i,t}) \;=\; \gamma_{y(i,t)} + \lambda_i F_t + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad y(i,t)=\text{first}_i+t,
$$ {#eq-yearfe}

by alternating between an OLS regression on year dummies and the hard-impute update of Section III.B. The resulting $\hat\gamma_y$ series is then scanned for an unknown structural break in Quandt--Andrews style: for each candidate year $\tau$, a piecewise-linear regression of $\hat\gamma_y$ on year, weighted by the number of underlying observations, tests for a slope shift at $\tau$, and a large $F$-statistic specifically within the 1993--2000 ICT-diffusion window would be direct evidence for the returns channel. Estimating (@eq-yearfe) on the full sample (1927--2016) and running this scan finds its largest slope break at **1983** ($F=114.2$), a magnitude far beyond chance given the number of candidates scanned, but every candidate in the 1991--2000 ICT window shows a markedly smaller, smoothly decaying $F$-statistic (44.9 at 1991 to 5.2 at 2000)---the statistical shadow of the 1983 break, not an independent second one. A break at 1983 predates ICT by roughly a decade; the number of distinct journals and observed author--age cells in the underlying corpus both show an independent break five years earlier (1977--1978, $F=564$--$568$), consistent with a Scopus indexing-coverage artifact rather than a behavioral shift, though the offset in timing means this is not a clean mechanical match. One auxiliary series does align with the ICT window: mean coauthors per paper shows an accelerating break at 1993--1997 ($F\approx73$), corroborating the team-size compositional shift above but not a discrete citation-level shock.

# Construct Validity: Nobel Laureate Verification {#sec-robustness}

To assess whether the estimated $\hat\alpha_i$ is a reasonable proxy for human capital, Nobel laureates in economics were matched to the sample by author identity. Of the 68 laureates recovered in the analytic sample, the mean $\hat\alpha_i$ percentile is 67.0 (against an expected value of 50 under random assignment). @tbl-nobel reports the distributional position of matched laureates in more detail.

| Percentile | Nobel matches | Share |
|------------|--------------:|------:|
| Top 1%     |             2 |  2.9% |
| Top 5%     |             8 | 11.8% |
| Top 10%    |             8 | 11.8% |
| Top 25%    |            30 | 44.1% |
| Top 50%    |            50 | 73.5% |

: Distributional position of Nobel laureates within the $\hat\alpha_i$ distribution {#tbl-nobel}

These results show that $\hat\alpha_i$ is associated with long-term assessments of academic excellence well above chance, though the fact that only 2.9% of matched laureates fall within the top 1% suggests that $\hat\alpha_i$, estimated from a 1970--2016 T6 sample restricted to authors with at least two distinct academic-age observations, is at best a noisy proxy for the very top of the ability distribution---consistent with the peer-environment caveat of Section VI.C, which indicates that a meaningful share of variation in $\hat\alpha_i$ is not attributable to stable individual ability alone.

# Discussion and Conclusion {#sec-discussion}

## Summary of Key Findings

This study estimates a time-invariant human-capital proxy for 9,843 researchers based on T6 economics journal publication histories, using an interactive fixed-effects factor model and a simpler additive alternative that is shown, via out-of-sample cross-validation, to perform equivalently and is therefore adopted as the primary estimator. The central finding is that this proxy is not a pure measure of individual ability: an early-career peer-environment design shows that the apparent benefit of strong local peers is entirely a between-institution artifact, and reverses sign once institution fixed effects remove that confound---exposure to an unusually strong contemporaneous peer cohort predicts *worse*, not better, long-run relative performance, consistent with congestion for scarce mentorship and collaboration resources rather than a positive ability spillover. Because the naive, pooled comparison alone would have pointed to the opposite conclusion, this reversal is also a methodological caution about inferring peer effects from panel fixed effects without a design that separates genuinely exogenous exposure from institutional sorting.

A secondary check of whether ICT diffusion reshaped the ability premium after 1992 finds a wider human-capital distribution among new entrants, concentrated among large-team collaborators, but no corresponding increase in the return to team size and no discrete calendar-year citation shock---evidence more consistent with a compositional shift in who enters T6 than with a clean returns- or threshold-channel effect, though these narrow tests do not rule out a more general change in the return to ability. The Nobel laureate verification supports the construct validity of the human-capital proxy in aggregate, while its imprecision at the very top of the distribution, together with the peer-environment finding, cautions that it should be interpreted as ability net of a non-trivial, resource-driven environmental component rather than as a pure measure of innate researcher quality.
